item.title: State of Understanding of High-speed Combustion: Can the Detonation Structure in Fuel-Air Mixtures Be Predicted?
item.description: arXiv:2611.28138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: (Abridged) High-speed reacting flows are central to many natural and practical systems, from detonation-based propulsion to various astrophysical phenomena. Here we discuss the limitations in our understanding of high-speed combustion by asking how well modern state-of-the-art physicochemical and computational models can predict the properties of a freely propagating detonation. We present a systematic survey of eleven fuel/air mixtures, from hydrogen, methane, acetylene, and ethylene to JP-10 and n-dodecane jet fuels, at a range of upstream pressures, temperatures, and equivalence ratios. Detonation properties are analyzed using prior numerical studies in the literature, as well as the multi-dimensional, high-fidelity simulations performed in this work, which employ modern multi-step kinetics based on the FFCM/HyChem families of reaction mechanisms. We show that simulations reproduce experimental cell sizes in H$_2$/air at sub-atmospheric pressures or elevated upstream temperatures, yet at the atmospheric conditions, disagreement in the predicted cell sizes is a factor of 3 - 6 at stoichiometric composition and much more severe in lean mixtures. Hydrocarbon fuels show comparable or even larger discrepancies. We argue that such disagreement cannot be ascribed solely to the computational factors, in particular, numerical resolution even at the continuum limit. We analyze the thermodynamic state space occupied by detonations in various mixtures, describe the predicted chemical properties in various regions of the state space, in particular ignition delays and their temperature sensitivity, and consider how well modern chemical kinetics mechanisms are constrained at these conditions by the direct ignition delay measurements. We further assess the proposed role of vibrational non-equilibrium and demonstrate that the current evidence is inconclusive. Finally, we summarize key open questions.

item.title: Nonpremixed Flames Near the Leading Edge of Parabolic Cylinders
item.description: arXiv:2611.28437v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonpremixed flames in the forward stagnation region of porous cylinders are classically described by the first-order stagnation-point boundary layer, which neglects the effects of surface curvature and boundary-layer displacement. In the present work, the description is extended to second order for a porous parabolic cylinder using the method of matched asymptotic expansions. The flame is assumed to be a sheet detached from the porous wall with unity Lewis numbers, and the model accounts for thermal expansion and displacement of the entire reacting layer. The expansion is verified against laminar Navier-Stokes solutions of the same idealized problem, and in the resolved cases the two-term errors decrease approximately as the square of the expansion parameter. At Reynolds numbers typical of laboratory-scale burners, curvature and displacement move the flame away from the wall and reduce the scalar dissipation rate, wall shear, and wall heat flux, whereas the flame temperature changes little. These effects increase with injection, and displacement contributes more over a longer porous section. The second-order terms considerably reduce the errors of the first-order theory in the flame stand-off distance and the scalar dissipation rate.
item.dc:creator: Vinicius M. Sauer, Jose M. Martinez

item.title: Distinguishing photothermal and photoelectrokinetic contributions to flow in light-activated microchannel architectures
item.description: arXiv:2611.28481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Light-driven flows near Janus surfaces could power microfluidic devices without external hardware. These flows are often attributed to photoinduced electro- or diffusio-osmosis, but illumination also heats the surface, potentially driving natural convection. Here, we map flow and temperature around a UVA-illuminated TiO$_2$-Au Janus membrane using depth-resolved particle tracking and infrared thermometry. Recirculating rolls form on both sides, with no measurable net flow across the membrane. Their cubic, reversing velocity profile identifies horizontal (Hadley) convection, driven by a lateral temperature gradient as the gold film absorbs light. The measured profile agrees with wall-corrected Hadley theory using one fitted parameter. Adding 100 mM NaCl to suppress electrokinetic flows leaves the profile unchanged, indicating that convection dominates. Simulations show that convection falls below 1 $\mu$m/s in thin channels, where surface-driven osmotic flows could dominate. Thus, device geometry and surface chemistry determine which mechanism governs light-driven microfluidic flows.

item.title: Numerical Study of Flow and Cavitation in Single-Liquid Injectors with Sharp-Edged and Chamfered Orifice Inlets
item.description: arXiv:2611.28527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the current work, the investigators used Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to investigate water flow and cavitation in single-liquid injectors with sharp-edged and chamfered orifice inlets. The k-{\omega} Shear Stress Transport (SST) turbulence model was used along with the Zwart-Gerber-Belamri (ZGB) cavitation model and the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method. The CFD predictions for the volumetric flow rate were validated against existing experimental data for the sharp-edged and chamfered orifice inlets. Pressure drops ranging between 0.07 MPa and 0.59 MPa were considered along with orifice length-to-diameter ratios of 2, 5, and 10. Strong cavitation was observed for the sharp-edged orifice inlet cases with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and a pressure drop larger than 0.2 MPa. A hydraulic flip was observed for the sharp-edged orifice inlet with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and a pressure drop of 0.59 MPa, which was consistent with the findings from the previous experimental study. Cavitation inception was observed for the chamfered orifice inlet cases with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and pressure drops larger than 0.2 MPa. For the sharp-edged orifice inlet with orifice length-to-diameter ratios of 2 and 10, a strong cavitation was observed inside the orifice.
item.dc:creator: Shreyash Gulati, Sven R. Walsberg, Timothy W. Nearhood, Jeffrey D. Moore

item.title: A Viscosity-Decoupled Uzawa Lattice Boltzmann Method for Incompressible Flows Across Reynolds Numbers
item.description: arXiv:2611.28609v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional lattice Boltzmann methods (LBMs) tie viscosity to collision relaxation, which induces diffusive stiffness at low Reynolds numbers, non-hydrodynamic instabilities at high Reynolds numbers, and passband breakdown in variable-relaxation dual-time schemes, whereas continuum incompressible solvers require global pressure-Poisson solves every step. We propose a Viscosity-Decoupled Uzawa Lattice Boltzmann Method (VDU-LBM) in D2Q9 and D3Q19 that permanently fixes collision at unit relaxation under smooth harmonic scaling and clears pre-collision non-conserved kinetic memory in one sweep. Constant, heterogeneous, and Smagorinsky eddy viscosities enter through a parameter-free post-streaming bond-symmetric momentum-flux lift that conserves discrete momentum pairwise without perturbing continuity. Variable-step BDF1/BDF2 marching is accelerated by a matrix-free local polynomial Uzawa smoother on the $(d+1)$ conserved moments, paired with link-wise Bouzidi curved walls and shifted ghost open boundaries. Across $\mathrm{Re}\in[10^{-4},10^6]$, VDU-LBM achieves smooth low-Mach second-order space--time accuracy, accelerates unsteady DFG 2D-2 shedding per cycle by $14.27\times\text{--}15.85\times$ over matched 20-core OpenFOAM-v2412, and lowers $256^3$ $\mathrm{Re}=1600$ resolved enstrophy error by $2.25\times$ versus hybrid recursive regularized LBM. On an NVIDIA A100 GPU, the fused D3Q19 solver attains $80.9\%\text{--}85.5\%$ of measured copy bandwidth in multi-pass port traffic and cuts bounded-relaxation diffusive step cost at high viscosity contrasts.
item.dc:creator: Yuan Yu, Yaolong Yu, Yanhui Ding

item.title: How Brine Pockets Evolve and Release in Ice
item.description: arXiv:2611.28699v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Liquid inclusions migrate through solids by melting at one end and freezing at the other, but how a macroscopic phase boundary regulates their deformation and release remains poorly understood. Here, we track individual brine pockets in saline ice through bulk migration, elongation, and release at the ice-water interface, resolving the motion of both ends. In the bulk, temperature-dependent thermomigration gradually elongates the pockets. Near the ice-water interface, the front slows, whereas liquid connection is followed by accelerated rear freezing and rapid shortening. These opposing responses arise from distinct changes in thermal-solutal transport: proximity to the boundary suppresses the local thermal-gradient enhancement and slows front-end melting, while liquid connection enables salt exchange with the surrounding liquid and accelerates rear-end freezing. A quasi-steady diffusion-resistance model captures the dependence of the half-length release time on the pocket length at connection and identifies an effective external exchange length consistent with a salt-balance estimate. Our results identify thermal proximity and liquid connectivity as distinct controls on inclusion evolution and release, providing a framework for understanding liquid redistribution in multicomponent solids.

item.title: Transient coupling of Marangoni spreading and interfacial waves
item.description: arXiv:2611.28784v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How does an initially non-uniform distribution of surfactant generate waves on a de- formable interface, and how do those waves then govern the redistribution of the surfactant? We answer this question for the linear Cauchy-Poisson problem of an axisymmetric interface between two viscous fluids, released from rest with independently prescribed distributions of surfactant and of interface displacement, by Hankel and Laplace transforms. In Stokes flow the pressure and the viscous normal stress of the Marangoni flow cancel in the nor- mal traction on the interface, for any viscosity ratio, so that the surfactant relaxes without displacing the interface: the coupling between surfactant redistribution and interface de- formation is inertial. With inertia, the Marangoni flow initiates a capillary-gravity wave whose polarity, at leading order for thin boundary layers, is set by the sign of $\rho_l \mu_l - \rho_u \mu_u $, and the surfactant is then carried by the wave, so that its concentration performs weakly damped oscillations at the wave frequency after the Marangoni relaxation of a flat surface has ended. The amplitude of these oscillations is given in closed form at small viscosity; its maximum does not coincide with that of the familiar resonant damping, and the surfactant and the interface shape decouple exactly only when the two fluids have equal densities and viscosities. A localized displacement radiates a wave packet that the surfactant damps, and a localized surfactant redistribution initiates a wave on an initially flat interface. Direct numerical simulations with sharp geometric surfactant transport verify these predictions.
item.dc:creator: Abhinandan Mohanty, Palas Kumar Farsoiya

item.title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Balancing Causation, Correlation, and User Intent
item.description: arXiv:2611.28794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Turbulence states vary widely in modeling difficulty, requiring distinct paradigms; thus, no single AI or data-driven approach suits all flows. We propose an operational framework classifying data-driven turbulence modeling by balancing physical causation and statistical correlation via non-equilibrium flow memory and user intent. Using the Mori--Zwanzig projection formalism, we decompose unclosed turbulent stress into a local response ($\tau_{ij}^L$) and a spatio-temporally non-local memory integral ($\tau_{ij}^{NL}$). Near statistical equilibrium, rapid relaxation suppresses advective memory, letting local correlations capture physical causation via intrusive $\tau_{ij}^L$ constitutive relations in Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations. Because the elliptic Poisson equation for fluctuating pressure couples stress evolution to eddy dimensionality beyond single-point velocity-gradient componentiality, local closures are not strictly valid even at equilibrium, yet remain acceptable engineering approximations. In non-equilibrium turbulence, modeling bifurcates by user intent. For predicting unseen geometries, large coherent structures sustain non-local memory ($\tau_{ij}^{NL}$), invalidating local total-stress closures and requiring first-principles causal scale resolution guided by Rules-Augmented AI (RAAI), with resolution set by a recent non-equilibrium theory. Conversely, for rapid design in a known, parameterized coherent flow class, a purely correlational strategy suffices: combining Non-Intrusive Reduced-Order Modeling (NIROM) with uncentered Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) across multi-realization ensembles yields zero-solver synthesis of stationary statistics and unsteady coherent evolution from governing dimensionless parameters. This framework aligns physical causation, statistical correlation, and user intent across flow regimes.
