item.title: Degenerate symmetric formulation and principal subsystems for chemically reacting multi-temperature fluid mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2611.28845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct a degenerate symmetric first-order formulation and principal subsystems for chemically reacting multi-temperature fluid mixtures with independent constituent velocities and temperatures, viscosity, and heat conduction. Starting from the entropy-admissible Class-III theory of arXiv:2610.37637, we characterize when its prescribed constituent Euler fluxes are generated by scalar potentials in the conservative entropy variables. Under the stated hypotheses the necessary and sufficient condition is that the separate Gibbs--Duhem one-forms $\omega_i$ vanish. This implies locally additive entropy, but it is not required by the general parent theory. In this subclass, the complete main field contains multipliers for both conservative balances and zero-storage constitutive equations. The spatial Hessians are symmetric, and the temporal Hessian is positive semidefinite and singular. For separated transport laws, eliminating auxiliary variables factorizes the positive-semidefinite dissipative principal symbol. We extend the algebraic Boillat--Ruggeri principal-subsystem construction to degenerate systems. Commuting restrictions yield a dissipative common-temperature system and a nested hierarchy of grouped-temperature Euler subsystems. Classical characteristic interlacing applies within the nested Euler hierarchy, whose temporal Hessians are positive definite. Separately, constrained entropy maximization defines an energy-equivalent common temperature and provides a thermodynamic Class-III-to-Class-II reduction for additive and nonadditive parent entropies. For a thermally reconstructed reference state, the full relative entropy splits exactly into the thermal projection deficit and the relative entropy of the retained variables. We derive the Class-II entropy-production identity and distinguish the thermodynamic projection from principal restrictions and dynamical relaxation limits.
item.dc:creator: Dieter Bothe, Tommaso Ruggeri

item.title: An Implicit Discrete Adjoint Unified Gas-Kinetic Scheme for Sensitivity Analysis and Shape Optimization in Multiscale Gas Flows
item.description: arXiv:2611.28923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate and efficient gradient-based sensitivity evaluation remains challenging for performance optimization in multiscale flows with complex geometries. To address this challenge, this work develops a matrix-free discrete adjoint method for the steady implicit unified gas-kinetic scheme (UGKS) through the exact linearization and transposition of its converged fixed-point operator. The method employs a hybrid differentiation strategy that combines local automatic differentiation (AD) of complex nonlinear kinetic kernels with analytically derived tangent and transpose operators for the coupled macroscopic--microscopic implicit updates and mass-conservation projection. This formulation ensures exact discrete consistency across both flow and geometric dependencies while avoiding global Jacobian assembly and the memory overhead of end-to-end reverse-mode AD. Verification tests across continuum, transitional, and free-molecular regimes confirm machine-precision stepwise duality with the corresponding tangent-linear solver and close agreement with central finite differences. In a six-parameter shape-sensitivity analysis, a single adjoint solve achieves speedups of 7.54X and 3.88X over tangent-linear and central finite-difference evaluations, respectively. Finally, constrained shape optimizations of a periodic Knudsen pump and a Mach-2 NACA0012 airfoil converge within ten design updates, achieving up to 29.68% improvement in normalized mass flow and 7.46% reduction in aerodynamic drag across internal and external multiscale flows.
item.dc:creator: Yuze Zhu, Hangkong Wu, Kun Xu

item.title: Fractal dimension of velocity-driven mixing: Reanalysis of Cao et al. (Phys. Rev. A 45, 3841 (1992)) and the universality of the Marstrand co-dimension rule
item.description: arXiv:2611.29053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cao et al. [Phys. Rev. A 45, 3841 (1992)] compared box-counting fractal dimensions of interfaces from continuum (SOLA-VOF) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of zero-Atwood-number mixing driven by random velocity perturbations. They reported D ~ 1.1-1.4 across physical models. We revisit their results with grid-converged geometric VOF simulations and modern box-counting algorithms. The grid-converged continuum dimension depends on the initial-condition realization (D = 1.13-1.38). Independent LAMMPS simulations show that Cao's MD dimension measures thermal scatter of atomic positions, not interface geometry, because their box-counting window lies below the scale of the interface structure: a flat interface at t=0 gives the same D ~ 1.36. When the thermal scatter is filtered by reducing the midpoint cloud to a curve (median binning at 2 sigma), the MD trajectory converges to the same late-time D ~ 1.43 as the continuum, recovering cross-model universality. We prove that the linear-regime box-counting dimension is exactly D = 2 - beta (A > 0) and D = 5/2 - beta (A = 0), where beta is the spectral exponent of the initial perturbation. For white noise (beta = 0) neither formula applies; Cao's early-time D ~ 2 is a boundary artifact. A three-dimensional grid convergence study gives D_3D = 2.361 +/- 0.002 at 400x400x200. Marstrand's co-dimension rule D_3D = D_2D + 1 shows a 7% discrepancy reflecting IC-realization dependence at A = 0, unlike the buoyancy-driven case where the discrepancy falls with resolution.
item.dc:creator: Rod W. Douglass, Steven R. Dunbar

item.title: OpenGLSA: A high-order matrix-free solver for global linear stability analysis of compressible flows on structured grids
item.description: arXiv:2611.29145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present OpenGLSA, an open-source code for the global linear stability analysis of compressible flows. It is based on a high-order finite-difference method on structured curvilinear grids and parallelised via the Message Passing Interface (MPI). The code supports linear stability analysis around planar and axisymmetric two-dimensional base flows with three-dimensional perturbations represented by Fourier mode expansions (BiGlobal), and on fully three-dimensional base flows (TriGlobal). Curvilinear coordinate grids are employed to facilitate flow analysis around complex geometries. Base flow computations employ the Selective Frequency Damping (SFD) method combined with weighted essentially non-oscillatory (WENO) reconstruction for shock capturing. A linearise-then-discretise approach is adopted for the linearised equations, and eigenmodes are computed using matrix-free time stepping coupled with the implicitly restarted Arnoldi method. This strategy significantly reduces memory requirements, thereby enhancing both the efficiency and tractability of memory-intensive compressible flow analyses. The solvers are validated against published results for low-Mach-number flows past a circular cylinder and a sphere, hypersonic flow over a compression ramp, and square and cubic lid-driven cavity flows.
item.dc:creator: Rui-Qing Yang, Bao-Feng Ma

item.title: Generation and characterization of unsteady inflows in a fan-vane wind tunnel
item.description: arXiv:2611.29228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wind-tunnel experiments often require inflows with specific combinations of turbulence intensity and integral length scale because both can influence the measured response. To broaden the range of attainable inflows, this study uses pseudorandom vane excitation to generate large-scale turbulence and examines how both quantities vary with the amplitude and spectral shape of the vane-angle command. In each test, the 15 servo-driven vanes downstream of a 768-fan array received the same angle command, and all fans operated at a common, constant duty cycle. Hot-wire measurements covered twenty heights and selected spanwise and downstream positions. At a fan-control duty cycle of 60%, increasing vane angular amplitude raised profile-mean turbulence intensity from 7.3% to 31.8% under periodic forcing and from 6.2% to 23.0% under pseudorandom forcing. With the normalized pseudorandom command spectrum held fixed, larger angular amplitudes increased the low-frequency share of velocity variance, accompanied by longer correlation times and larger integral scales. At a root-mean-square angular amplitude of 15 degrees, changing the command spectrum yielded profile-mean integral length scales of 0.88-1.67 m at similar turbulence intensities. The principal features of the velocity spectra persisted between 2 and 4 m downstream, while integral scales continued to change. Both forcing types exhibited middle-region minima in turbulence intensity and integral scale. Regional analysis of a representative pseudorandom case linked these minima to weaker low-frequency fluctuations and shorter correlation times. These findings provide a basis for selecting vane inputs according to the turbulence-intensity and integral-scale requirements of the intended test region.
item.dc:creator: Yutong Liu, Gang Hu, Hongwei Zhang

item.title: Transient Impact Force and Spreading Dynamics of Droplets Impacting Spherical Surfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.29371v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Droplet impacts on spherical surfaces are encountered in processes such as spray cooling, anti-icing, and spray deposition. The curvature of the impact target changes the spreading path of the droplet and the impact force, leading to more complex kinematic and transient force dynamics. This study employs a numerical model utilizing the volume of fluid approach to investigate the spreading, retraction, rebound and deposition characteristics of droplets impinging on spherical surfaces. The roles of wall wettability, spherical curvature, Weber number, and Ohnesorge number on droplet spreading and wall impact force are analyzed. The results show that the wall impact force exhibits two peaks in the complete rebound and partial rebound modes, whereas the second peak disappears in the complete deposition mode. Further parametric analysis shows that increasing the contact angle, i.e., decreasing wettability, reduces both the maximum spreading length and the contact time, and significantly changes the second peak of the impact force. Under complete rebound mode, the relationship between the contact time and the contact angle can be expressed as ${{{t}_{\text{c}}}}/{{{t}_{\sigma }}}\;={{C}_{1}}\left[ {{\left( 1-\cos {{\theta }_{\text{eq}}} \right)}^{{-1}/{2}\;}}-{1}/{\sqrt{2}} \right]+{{C}_{2}}$, where $C_1$ and $C_2$ are constants. Within the investigated curvature range, increasing the dimensionless curvature reduces the critical contact angle required for complete rebound. The dimensionless first peak of the impact force decreases with increasing the Weber number and finally approaches a constant, following a relationship of $F_{\text{t}1}^{*}={{\beta }_{1}}+{{\beta }_{2}}W{{e}^{-1}}$, where ${{\beta }_{1}}$ and ${{\beta }_{2}}$ are constants. Increasing the Ohnesorge number reduces the maximum spreading length, prolongs the contact time, and slightly increases the first peak of impact force.
item.dc:creator: Mengqi Ye, Tianyou Wang, Zhizhao Che

item.title: Dynamic Renewal for Hydrodynamic Coupling in Ciliary Mucus Transport
item.description: arXiv:2611.29378v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mucociliary clearance in large mammalian airways involves millimetric MUC5B-rich mucus strands that emerge from submucosal glands approximately aligned with the direction of transport. These strands are observed downstream in cross-flow networks. Recently, Bos et al. [PNAS Nexus 2, pgad388 (2023)] modeled single strand reorientation using a free-draining coupling for the flow induced by cilia. This leaves unresolved whether the strand's own disturbance of the surrounding liquid assists or frustrates the turning. Here, we develop the methodology to address this question. An immersed-boundary coupling is combined with a Fourier-space Stokes solver and a bespoke dynamic-renewal algorithm that exposes the strand to new ciliary domain without enlarging the simulation volume. This allows us to overcome one of the multiscale challenges posed by mucociliary clearance. We find that hydrodynamic interactions result in only a limited decrease in the rate of reorientation, which supports the use of the free-draining approximation. Future work can build on the methodological foundation introduced here to study collective strand dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Jeroen Bechtold, Valentijn van Zwieten, Iris Verkuil, Meike F. Bos, Georg Rempfer, Mae Nesenberend, Pieter Michels, Florian K. R. Gaeremynck, Bart Stam, Debabrata Panja, Joost de Graaf

item.title: Stable eigenmodes of the Large-scale circulation in Turbulent Convection
item.description: arXiv:2611.29636v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Turbulent Rayleigh-B\'enard convection (RBC) is a canonical system for studying buoyancy-driven turbulence. Its defining feature is a system-size large-scale circulation (LSC), whose dynamics reflect the coupling between coherent motion and turbulent fluctuations. Starting from the Boussinesq Navier-Stokes and temperature equations, we derive three coupled stochastic equations for the LSC angular velocity and its associated dipolar temperature field. The deterministic dynamics contain an unstable no-LSC set and two symmetry-related stable finite-LSC states. Linearization about either finite-LSC state yields one purely relaxational eigenmode and a pair of damped oscillatory eigenmodes whose frequency is set by the LSC turnover rate. Turbulent fluctuations continually excite the latter, providing a dynamical origin for the observed quasi-periodic oscillations. Experiments in a thin-disk cell directly resolve both eigenmodes and show their predicted Rayleigh-number scalings. The same stochastic dynamics also provide a route to rare cessations and reversals. This theory-experiment framework provides a tractable example of how coherent circulation states, intrinsic modes, and fluctuation-driven transitions emerge in turbulent convection, with broader relevance to geophysical and astrophysical flows.
item.dc:creator: Yin Wang, Pik-Yin Lai, Penger Tong

item.title: Experimental study of the Reynolds number effect on the mean flow and coherent structures in a 180-degree bent pipe flow using PIV
item.description: arXiv:2611.29694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we study the effect of Reynolds number on the flow in a 180{\deg} pipe bend with a curvature of {\gamma} = 0.2. We perform planar particle image velocimetry (PIV) in the symmetry plane of the pipe for bulk Reynolds numbers ReD from 10 000 to 60 000 with water as the working fluid. To remove the refraction at the pipe wall, a hybrid method is employed. A mixture of water, glycerol and sodium iodide is used to match the refractive index of the pipe at its outer interface. The refraction at the inner interface is corrected using reverse ray tracing. The measurements are validated against direct numerical simulations at ReD = 10 000 and 20 000 and against hot-wire data from the literature at 60 000. As the Reynolds number increases, the mean velocity profiles in and downstream of the bend become flatter. Furthermore, a second vortex pair, with the opposite direction of rotation to the Dean vortices, forms further downstream, between bend angles of 116{\deg} and 126{\deg}. A modal decomposition of the planar velocity fields shows that the coherent structures keep their spatial features at all Reynolds numbers. Their Strouhal numbers remain nearly unchanged and show no monotonic trend.
item.dc:creator: Eman Bagheri, Christoph Heigl, Felix Czwielong, Stefan Becker, Philipp Schlatter

item.title: Collision of a sphere and a prolate spheroid settling in a quiescent ambient
item.description: arXiv:2611.29733v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The collision rate of a prolate spheroid and a sphere settling through a quiescent fluid at small Reynolds number is computed for randomly oriented spheroids and for spheroids turned broadside by weak fluid inertia. Without hydrodynamic interactions, the collision cross-section is the projection of the spheroid enlarged by the radius of the sphere. The ideal kernel then follows in closed form for aligned spheroids and from a one-dimensional quadrature for isotropic ones. Alignment raises the ideal kernel by at most a factor of 4/{\pi}, but extinguishes it on the extinction locus, where an isolated broadside spheroid settles as fast as the sphere. Hydrodynamic interactions are computed from pair trajectories in a first-reflection slender-body model, in which the interaction velocity is proportional to the difference of the buoyant weights and only the flow of the sphere rotates the spheroid. A strongly aligned spheroid weathervanes, whereas a freely rotating one feathers and glides. Weathervaning lowers the collision efficiency, as does feathering far from the extinction locus, but gliding raises it near the locus. There, the collision rate of spheroids aligned at a finite rate lies far above both the strong-alignment result and the ideal isotropic kernel. Just above the extinction locus, where strongly aligned spheroids are blocked, collisions persist at all the finite alignment rates computed. A boundary-element solution shows that the model overestimates the rate at which the gap closes near contact. A lubrication film largely corrects this and reduces the collision efficiencies from their interception values. Simple fits for the ideal kernels, the efficiencies and the near-contact correction are provided for use in collision models.
item.dc:creator: Arnab Choudhury, Anubhab Roy

item.title: Scalable Modal Analysis of the Imperial Front Wing Flow Field
item.description: arXiv:2611.29995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The aerodynamic performance of motorsport vehicles relies on understanding the unsteady flow dynamics around complex geometries at high Reynolds numbers. Extracting the dominant 3D coherent structures from high-fidelity simulations is often intractable due to the high dimensionality of the state-space, and standard modal decompositions, such as proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), do not give interpretable meaning to the temporal dynamics of the modes. This study demonstrates a scalable POD and Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) method, implemented in the open-source pyLOM framework, that can identify coherent structures and their temporal dynamics in high-fidelity simulations of Formula 1 aerodynamics, specifically the Imperial Front Wing (IFW), a publicly available benchmark based on the McLaren MP4-17D, at Reynolds number $Re = 2.2 \times 10^5$. DMD is applied to large eddy simulation (LES) results of the flow field that is resolved using spectral/hp element method via Nektar++, producing $49.72 \times 10^6$ degrees of freedom at polynomial order p=4. The simulation captures four dominant vortical structures (endplate, canard, main, and footplate), with time-averaged force coefficients showing 2.24% and 2.87% differences in $C_L$ and $C_D$ compared to the reference data. DMD extracts the frequencies, amplitudes and damping ratios of the coherent structures, and modes at chord-based Strouhal numbers of 5.1, 7.5 and 9.3 are associated, through point-probe spectra, with the main-element laminar separation bubble, canard vortex core pulsation and endplate vortex meander, respectively. The DMD allows for both a model reduction technique and a compression scheme, here reducing approximately 6 TB of snapshots to 200 GB of modal data.
item.dc:creator: Parv Khurana, Benet Eiximeno, Alexandra Liosi, Spencer Sherwin, Athanasios Chatzopoulos, Julien Hoessler, Arnau Mir\'o, Oriol Lehmkuhl, Ivette Rodriguez, J. Nathan Kutz

item.title: A Steady Theory for Highly Unsteady Thin Airfoil Motions
item.description: arXiv:2611.30074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A generalized steady thin airfoil theory is built not from steady flow, but from flows in which there exists a frame of reference where the absolute vorticity field is steady. We specialize this general idea to construct a foliation of a domain of phase space for thin airfoil motions in which staying on a leaf of the foliation maintains zero absolute vorticity in the fluid indefinitely. The phase space is described by the airfoil's total rotation rate, speed, and angle of attack. It is found using this definition that one of the preeminent unsteady stall conditions is equivalent to the traditional steady stall condition for this class of flows, various other classical results can be re-interpreted as steady in the absolute vorticity field, and insight is also provided into the surprising experimental results of McGowan et al. (AIAA J. 49, 2011). We show parts of existing quasi-steady flow and Theodorsen unsteady flow theory can be built from a planar approximation of our foliation, making the quasi-steady extension of our theory trivial, and suggesting how an unsteady extension can be created as well. Furthermore, pure unsteady effects in the new theory amount to a transversal of the leaves, occupying just one dimension, inviting interesting prospects for future experimental and theoretical work.
item.dc:creator: Scott A. Bollt

item.title: Flow-induced vibration of an array of circular cylinders in a square enclosure due to thermal buoyancy
item.description: arXiv:2611.30091v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flow-induced oscillations of heated cylinder arrays in a square enclosure driven solely by natural convection are investigated in the current study at Prandtl number of 7 and Raleigh number of $10^7$ (based on side of square enclosure). This is accomplished by a coupled thermal-fluid-structure-interaction formulation based on body-fitted arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian framework, implemented using variational finite element methodology. Study on stationary array shows asymmetry in the $3\times 3$ configuration, along with a non-dimensional wall-gap plume oscillation frequency of 0.183 on the left column cylinders. When elastically mounted, these cylinders synchronize and lock-in with the frequency at reduced velocity of 15.7. The remaining cylinders undergo broadband buffeting that grows monotonically with reduced velocity and exceeds the synchronized response. The $4\times 4$ array shows symmetric behavior with no synchronization. The response is observed to be forced buffeting for all the cylinders, and dominated by the slow plume forcing for the inner column cylinders. The motion of the cylinders also influence the heat transfer characteristics. The $3\times 3$ array shows negligible change in heat transfer for the whole array, while measurable enhancement is observed for $4\times 4$ array.
item.dc:creator: Amit Pramod Joshi, Nishit Gupta, Unnat Agarwal, Vaibhav Joshi

item.title: Spatial dimensionality affects the convective thawing of permafrost
item.description: arXiv:2611.30306v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Permafrost thaw is one of the major consequences of ongoing climate change, with potentially far-reaching implications for high-latitude and high-altitude environments. Because permafrost degradation is a subsurface phenomenon, its dynamics and future evolution are primarily investigated through numerical models. Yet, the role of groundwater convection in permafrost thawing is an underrepresented process. Here, we explore how the spatial dimensionality affects the simulation of permafrost thaw and heat transport within the thawed layer, known as the active layer. Using two- and three-dimensional (2D and 3D) simulations, with realistic parameter sets that enable convection, we show that permafrost thawing rate and heat transport are systematically slower in 2D than in 3D simulations. The ice-water interface develops spatial patterns that coincides with the underlying convective structures, with rising cold plumes and descending warm plumes shaping its morphology. These findings reveal a coupling between convective flow structures and the evolving geometry of the permafrost boundary, and highlight the importance of three-dimensional representations of subsurface heat transport for accurately capturing permafrost thaw dynamics in land-surface models.
item.dc:creator: M. Magnani, S. Musacchio, G. Boffetta

item.title: Oceanic Surface Waves from Wind-Drift-Layer Instability: Exponential Growth to Finite-Amplitude States
item.description: arXiv:2611.30456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Oceanic wind-wave genesis via shear-induced linear instability and the propagation and breaking of finite-amplitude waves have traditionally been studied as decoupled problems. While experimental evidence indicates connection between the two regimes, a first principles demonstration that the latter can emerge from the former remains challenging. Here, we bridge this gap by investigating gravity-dominated surface waves arising from an inviscid, shear-driven Holmboe instability. The background state comprises a uniform air current and a constant-vorticity water drift layer of finite thickness overlying deep irrotational water. In the high-Bond-number and low-Froude-number regime, this configuration supports Holmboe-unstable modes beyond a critical Froude number. Two-phase simulations of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, initialised with the fastest-growing eigenmode, exhibit initial exponential growth in excellent agreement with linear theory. In the subsequent nonlinear stage preceding breaking, finite-amplitude propagating waveforms develop. Spatio-temporal spectral analysis reveals bound harmonics locked to the primary carrier wave, coexisting with residual free-wave components. This indicates that an infinitesimal, linearly unstable mode can evolve into a nonlinear propagating waveform of approximately permanent form under background shear. To characterise these waveforms theoretically, we formulate an exact nonlinear boundary-value problem for steady-state propagating waves including background shear. The resulting wave profiles show very good agreement with time-averaged profiles extracted from the transient simulations in the nonlinear stage. These findings extend the existing theory and complement the wind-wave observations, demonstrating that sheared Stokes-like waves, can naturally emerge during the nonlinear evolution of a wind-drift-induced linear instability.
item.dc:creator: Sayali N. Jadhav, S. Ravichandran, Ratul Dasgupta

item.title: Discrete adjoint method for the general synthetic iterative scheme for optimization of rarefied and continuum gas flows
item.description: arXiv:2611.30491v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A discrete adjoint method is developed for the general synthetic iterative scheme (GSIS) to enable efficient gradient-based optimization of gas flows across rarefied and continuum regimes. The primal GSIS is expressed as a fixed-point system of kinetic and macroscopic synthetic equations, and both sets of residuals are incorporated into a discrete Lagrangian. Imposing stationarity of this Lagrangian then yields a coupled mesoscopic-macroscopic adjoint system that directly inherits the primal acceleration structure, without a separate Chapman-Enskog or asymptotic analysis. The resulting system is solved by alternating kinetic and macroscopic updates analogous to those in the primal GSIS, with the inner subproblems treated using established discrete adjoint techniques for the discrete velocity method and Navier-Stokes equations. Tests on the NACA0012 airfoil show that adjoint sensitivities closely agree with central finite-difference estimates, while the adjoint solver achieves convergence efficiency comparable to that of the primal GSIS, with both solvers converging within tens of iterations in rarefied and near-continuum flows. The method is further validated by multi-objective shape optimization and boundary-flow-parameter optimization. For a three-dimensional re-entry capsule, shape optimization reduces peak wall heat flux by 14.17%, 10.68%, and 6.54% while achieving respective lift-to-drag gains of 10%, 20%, and 25%. For a fixed-geometry showerhead chamber, optimization of inlet-flow allocation reduces the coefficient of variation of wafer pressure from 1.49% to 0.06% at fixed total gas supply, while maintaining the mean pressure near its initial value. Beyond these applications, the formulation provides a systematic and extensible framework for constructing multiscale adjoint solvers directly from the fixed-point representations of their primal counterparts.
item.dc:creator: Jianan Zeng, Ruifeng Yuan, Wei Su

item.title: Spontaneous Axis-Switching Swirling in Transonic Core-Annular Flow of Highly Differentiated Fluids
item.description: arXiv:2611.30823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forcing fluids to interact at high speeds creates a multitude of instabilities. Prior studies considered the consequences of these instabilities for core-annular flow (CAF) or atomization systems. However, the existence of spontaneous axis-switching swirling (SASS) modalities in CAF have never been explored. We computationally demonstrate this new behavior for a CAF of steam surrounded by a cold non-Newtonian fuel. Wave pile-up created 3-D fuel surface disturbances which eventually became thin slender lobes with radial modal deformation. Those slender lobes were subject to further instabilities and resulted in oscillatory tangential velocities that were a large fraction of the core steam velocity and orthogonal to the axially flowing base fuel wave. Since these tangential velocities were not externally imposed by atomizer geometry or boundary conditions, it was concluded that they are self-generating. Frequency analysis revealed that SASS tended to operate at the base wave frequency. We additionally explored numerical uncertainty with our previously validated computational tool and found that SASS behavior can be achieved on a coarse, limited mesh at relatively low simulation times.
item.dc:creator: Wayne Strasser, Aleck Tilbrook, Daniel Wilson

item.title: Compressibility effects on the flow-induced motions of bluff bodies: common features from transverse and rotary oscillations
item.description: arXiv:2611.30903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compressibility effects on flow-induced motions of bluff bodies are examined through two-dimensional direct numerical simulations of undamped transverse vortex-induced vibration (TVIV) of a circular cylinder ($Re=150$) and vortex-induced rotary oscillation (VIRO) of an elliptic cylinder of aspect ratio $0.5$ ($Re=200$) for free-stream Mach numbers $0.1\leq M_{\infty}\leq 0.6$. Response characteristics are analyzed across the first desynchronized zone ($DS\text{-}I$), the synchronous (lock-in) branch ($SB$), and the second desynchronized zone ($DS\text{-}II$). While compressibility effects are noted to stabilize the oscillations in $SB$ in terms of reductions in response amplitudes and fluctuating aerodynamic coefficients, as well as the extent and intensity of hysteretic jumps, in contrast, the oscillation amplitudes and aerodynamic coefficients increase with $M_{\infty}$ in $DS\text{-}II$, where the amplitude variation with $M_{\infty}$ is shown to follow the \textit{modified Prandtl-Glauert relationship} for both TVIV and VIRO cases. This indicates the role of the inviscid nature of compressibility in the $DS\text{-}II$ regime in increasing the oscillation response, as opposed to $SB$ where enhanced viscous stabilization with increasing $M_{\infty}$ leads to the moderation of response. Although the simulations are performed at low Reynolds numbers, the identified trends are consistent with fundamental compressibility mechanisms and may therefore persist at higher Reynolds numbers.
item.dc:creator: Sawant Omkar Deepak, Swagata Bhaumik

item.title: Density-ratio invariance of the optimal passive pitching of a self-propelled three-dimensional flapper
item.description: arXiv:2611.30979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study numerically a 3D flapper of finite span that propels itself by a prescribed sinusoidal heaving motion of its centre of mass, while pitching passively. We vary the stiffness of the spring for three solid-to-fluid density ratios, $\rho_p/\rho_f=1$, 10 and 100. For all three cases, the propulsive speed reaches approximately the same maximum, while the stiffness at which it occurs increases with the density ratio. When the stiffness is shifted by the respective optimum, the propulsive speeds of the three density ratios collapse onto a single curve. At the optimum, the three flappers pitch with the same amplitude and lead the heaving motion by $113^\circ$, so that they experience the same effective angle of attack and the same vertical hydrodynamic force. The passive pitching acts as a feathering motion that turns the flapper towards the incoming flow. Stiffer springs feather too little, so the effective angle of attack remains large, the flow separates at the leading and trailing edges, and the hydrodynamic force acts mainly in the heaving direction. Softer springs result in excessive and delayed pitching of the flapper, and the benefits of feathering are outweighed by weaker hydrodynamic forces. The optimum balances these two limits. The input power increases with the density ratio because of the inertia of the flapper, so that the distance travelled per unit input work decreases, whereas the propulsive efficiency, which accounts for the kinetic energy of the flapper, shows the opposite trend. A comparison with the resonant stiffness of the flapper considering the added inertia of quiescent fluid, shows that the optimal spring is stiffer than the resonant one for all density ratios, by a nearly constant amount. The optimal spring is therefore not set by resonance but by the feathering motion it produces, and a flapper of higher density ratio only needs a stiffer spring to reach it.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Schenk, Manuel Garcia-Villalba, Manuel Moriche

item.title: Hydrodynamic interactions of self-propelled tandem flappers with passive pitching
item.description: arXiv:2611.31028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We simulate two in-line, self-propelled 3D flappers of finite span, driven by sinusoidal heaving motions with a phase difference $\Delta \phi$. Pitching is passive, governed by fluid--structure interaction and resisted by a torsional spring. We first consider identical spring stiffnesses, set to the value that maximises the propulsive speed of an isolated flapper. We characterise the self-arrangement of the pair. The pair settles into a stable equilibrium for all phase shifts, travelling at a common propulsive speed and maintaining an equilibrium distance that increases approximately linearly with $\Delta \phi$. The leader is largely unaffected by the presence of the follower and performs similarly to an isolated flapper, whereas the follower requires more power in every case. This additional power outweighs the small increase in propulsive speed, so that the tandem generally provides no efficiency benefit over an isolated flapper, with comparable efficiency reached only at an intermediate phase shift. For equal stiffness, the power penalty of the follower is associated with a reduction of its pitching amplitude by the wake of the leader, while its pitching phase remains nearly unchanged relative to the isolated flapper. Keeping the leader at the stiffness that maximises its isolated propulsive speed, we investigate whether the tandem performance can be improved by independently tuning the follower through the stiffness ratio $\tilde{\kappa}$ in the range $0.8 \le \tilde{\kappa} \le 1.2$. Reducing the follower stiffness lowers its power requirement and increases the tandem efficiency by an almost phase-independent amount, without affecting the equilibrium distance or propulsive speed significantly. For the softest follower considered, the tandem is more efficient than an isolated flapper across the full range of phase shifts, with gains of about 2--3\% for $\Delta \phi \ge 90^\circ$
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Schenk, Gonzalo Arranz, Oscar Flores, Manuel Moriche, Manuel Garcia-Villalba

item.title: Modeling of reactive porosity waves as a fluid release process in a dehydrating slab
item.description: arXiv:2611.31131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dehydration of subducting serpentinites releases aqueous fluids that must be efficiently extracted from the slab. We present a fully coupled two-dimensional hydro--mechanical--chemical model of reactive porosity waves in deforming and dehydrating serpentinite. Thermodynamic closure is provided by Gibbs free-energy minimization for the MgO--FeO--SiO$_2$--H$_2$O system, including dissolved SiO$_2$ in the aqueous phase. Natural multiscale compositional maps of serpentinites from the Mirdita ophiolite (Albania) are used to prescribe initial SiO$_2$ and FeO heterogeneities. The simulations show that these intrinsic chemical variations trigger spontaneous localization of porosity and fluid flow during dehydration, without prescribing channel geometry. Channelization results from the coupling of decompaction, fluid-pressure buildup, buoyancy-driven flow, and metasomatic reactions associated with infiltration of SiO$_2$-poor hydrous fluid and olivine formation. The resulting fluid-rich channels propagate upward and develop connected networks resembling natural vein systems. Our results demonstrate that reactive porosity waves in compositionally heterogeneous serpentinites provide a robust mechanism for focusing fluid flow and enhancing fluid extraction from dehydrating subducting slabs.
item.dc:creator: Liudmila Khakimova, Konstantin Huber, Yury Y. Podladchikov, Johannes C. Vrijmoed, Boris Antonenko, Timm John

item.title: Vortex rings shape the feeding-efficiency landscape of jellyfish
item.description: arXiv:2611.31170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fluid flows enable and limit the feeding and locomotion of sea creatures across a wide range of scales. Although much is known about how microorganisms navigate life at low Reynolds numbers, the effect of inertial flows on the feeding-efficiency of larger marine organisms remains less well understood. Here, using jellyfish as an archetypal example, we study the trade-off between prey capture rate and energy expended to generate inertial flows by surface deformations. We develop a feeding-efficiency landscape that predicts an optimal feeding regime at the transition from Stokes pumping to inertial prey transport, mediated by a self-generated vortex ring. These predictions provide a unifying biophysical explanation of size and beat frequencies reported for jellyfish species from different taxa, with vortex-ring-dominated transport supported by our experimental observations for the moon jellyfish \textit{Aurelia aurita}. More broadly, our results demonstrate how centimetric marine predators can exploit inertial flows for efficient prey capture.
item.dc:creator: Harry Walden, Ashutosh Tripathi, Teo Lara, Brandon Weissbourd, J\"orn Dunkel

item.title: A centered finite-volume method with explicit pressure relaxation for weakly compressible single- and two-phase flows
item.description: arXiv:2611.31197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a non-dissipative centered finite-volume method for weakly compressible single- and two-phase flows. The method couples kinetic-energy-preserving advection to conservative diffuse-interface regularization and explicit pressure relaxation on structured collocated grids. To control excessive phase-mass outflow when neighboring cells have different intrinsic densities, we construct phase-mass fluxes using harmonic face densities. This connects phase-volume and phase-mass transport without altering the advective kinetic-energy identity, yielding a sufficient positivity condition and an inverse-density transport identity at finite velocity divergence. To retain the benefit of low-dissipation transport in the coupled calculation, a pressure-increment formulation incorporates the existing pressure gradient in the predictor. Compatible cell and face operators give a conditional energy estimate for additional pressure iterations, while fully discrete budgets separate advection, predictor pressure work, and the final correction. In inviscid homogeneous isotropic turbulence on $128^3$ cells, the relative kinetic-energy change remains below $1.2\times10^{-7}$ in magnitude at $t^*=8$ in both single-phase and density-ratio-$1000$ two-phase calculations. Matched upwind calculations retain only $3.60\%$ and $30.72\%$ of their initial energies, respectively. Shear layers, cavities, rising bubbles, and dam breaks demonstrate applicability to incompressible-regime flows. In a three-dimensional dam break, harmonic averaging retains positive phase masses where arithmetic averaging produces negative values. With centered advection, a prescribed subgrid-scale stress supplies the principal dissipation. The local pressure algorithm and collocated finite-volume form support future large-scale multiphase large-eddy simulation on GPUs with adaptive mesh refinement.
item.dc:creator: Shintaro Matsushita, Suhas S. Jain, Andrei G. Fedorov, Tetsuya Suekane

item.title: Flood forecasting using a physics-guided conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model
item.description: arXiv:2611.31212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-resolution flood forecasting with full two-dimensional shallow water equation (SWE) solvers remains computationally expensive, even on GPUs. We develop a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that forecasts the evolution of 30 m water-depth fields over a four-day horizon for the Des Plaines River watershed, Illinois. The model is trained on SynxFlow SWE simulations of 113 historical storms observed across twelve Midwestern states (2003-2024), each under three antecedent-wetness scenarios, and can optionally be conditioned on coarse 100 m or 150 m hydrodynamic simulations. Because reverse diffusion is stochastic, every forecast is a 20-member ensemble drawn from the same trained model. Coarse conditioning reduces the four-day mean water-depth RMSE of the ensemble mean from 0.170 m to 0.054 m (100 m) and 0.048 m (150 m). The coarser 150 m conditioning also gives the best critical success index (0.839), false alarm ratio, CRPS and Brier score at lower cost, so finer conditioning does not guarantee better skill. Averaging members reduces error by 5-11% relative to a single realization, and the ensemble provides spatially explicit exceedance probabilities, although the ensembles are under-dispersive (spread-to-error ratios 0.35-0.73). On a single GPU, a four-day forecast over 26 non-overlapping patches is 7.8x, 11.0x and 16.3x faster than the 30 m simulation for the 100 m, 150 m and unconditioned configurations, and projected speedups for a 14-day forecast reach 12-49x for one member and 48-58x for 20 members. Physics-guided diffusion models are thus promising probabilistic surrogates for regional-scale flood forecasting.
item.dc:creator: Omar Sallam, David Coe, Jeremy Feinstein, Hugo Torres, Sofia Sahagun Covarrubias, Eugene Yan

item.title: Shallow may be better: Physics-Constrained Lightweight Networks for High-Throughput Particle Image Velocimetry
item.description: arXiv:2611.28088v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Convolutional networks for optical flow typically adopt progressively deeper pyramidal encoders under the assumption that larger receptive fields improve motion estimation. For particle image velocimetry (PIV), however, tracer-particle displacement between frames is bounded by the acquisition geometry, allowing network depth to be derived from the physically admissible displacement rather than inherited from general-purpose architectures. Using a layer-by-layer analysis of spatial-support growth, we derive its explicit upper bound and show that deeper architectures substantially exceed the support required for PIV, compromising training stability, spatial resolution under particle loss, and inference efficiency. Based on this analysis, we develop LIMA3, a lightweight pyramidal displacement estimator with 589,000 trainable parameters. Across synthetic and experimental benchmarks, LIMA3 matches the accuracy of established learned and classical methods with at least an order of magnitude less memory and substantially higher throughput, while retaining the physically expected coarsening of spatial resolution as tracer information is lost. Its linear memory scaling enables megapixel processing within embedded memory budgets, such that LIMA3 can reach over 900 image pairs per second at $640\times480$~pixel on an RTX 5090 and 99 image pairs per second on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. The spatial-support analysis provides a transferable design principle for compact optical-flow architectures and bounded-window attention, offering an alternative to compressing oversized general-purpose networks and enabling efficient operation alongside image acquisition.
item.dc:creator: Claudio Mucignat, Kamila Zdybal, Ivan Lunati

item.title: Failure Modes and Data-Efficient Remedies for Transformer-Based Prediction of Viscoplastic Flows
item.description: arXiv:2611.28267v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fast and accurate prediction of viscoplastic flows remains a challenge in computational rheology due to yield surfaces, discontinuous gradients, and strongly nonlinear transitions between yielded and unyielded regions. Transformer-based neural operators such as RheOFormer have recently shown strong potential for surrogate modeling of non-Newtonian flows. However, their applicability to viscoplastic systems and their efficacy in recovering realistic flows remain poorly understood. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of RheOFormer applied to steady Bingham channel flow. By isolating the problem to a simple geometry and constitutive model, we examine how dataset structure, numerical value range, and input representation govern the model's ability to interpolate and extrapolate within the parameter space. The data regimes in which RheOFormer remains accurate and those in which errors emerge are identified, particularly for plug-dominated flows and for conditions outside the velocity scales or flow structures represented during training. Upon identifying these failure modes, targeted enhancements to the input representation and loss formulation are introduced to better predict low-gradient plug regions. Logarithmic velocity representations and gradient-aware loss formulations substantially improve accuracy in challenging regimes where the baseline formulation fails. In addition, extrapolation errors are reduced by augmenting the training set with only a few strategically selected cases spanning the missing physical regimes. Finally, a single partially developed snapshot suffices for an accurate steady-state prediction, and the model outperforms simply copying its input throughout flow development. These results highlight the importance of appropriate field representation and parameter-space coverage for data-efficient neural-operator prediction of viscoplastic flows.
item.dc:creator: Maedeh Saberi, Hugo Franca, Maziyar Jalaal, Safa Jamali

item.title: A scalar arterial input function does not uniquely determine the perfusion residue: Theory and phantom MRI
item.description: arXiv:2611.28378v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Purpose: To relate the residue function of tracer kinetic models to blood velocity and cross-sectional tracer distributions at the arterial inlet, and show that a cross-sectionally averaged arterial input function (AIF) does not uniquely determine the residue. Theory and Methods: For steady laminar flow without radial diffusion, the residue function referenced to the cross-sectionally averaged inlet AIF was analytically derived from the velocity and inlet tracer distributions. In a straight tube with parabolic flow, two nonnegative inlet profiles sharing one measured AIF were compared for gamma-variate and rectangular arterial spin labeling (ASL) inputs. A straight-tube phantom was imaged at 3 T during gadolinium bolus passage, with uniform fills as controls. Results: In the phantom, enhancement during bolus arrival was greater near the lumen center than near the wall at all 11 stations and for all three boluses, whereas uniform gadolinium fills showed no such pattern. In the tube model, the two profiles produced tissue curves differing by up to 23.3% of the uniform-inlet peak and 0.30 s in time to peak for the gamma-variate input, and by 33.3% for ASL labels shorter than the fastest transit time. Their residues differed in initial amplitude and normalized temporal shape. Conclusion: Identical AIFs can produce different tissue concentration curves, depending on the spatial distributions of inlet tracer concentration and arterial flow velocity. Consequently, the residue-AIF tracer kinetic models may not be consistent with fluid mechanics or interpreted as tissue flow.
item.dc:creator: Yuyang Gan, Dominick Romano, Maneesh John, Renjiu Hu, Qihao Zhang, Benjamin Weppner, Alexey V. Dimov, Pascal Spincemaille, Yi Wang

item.title: An Annular Spiral Construction for Anomalous Dissipation in the Forced Navier-Stokes Equations
item.description: arXiv:2611.29458v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Kolmogorov's 1941 theory of turbulence (K41) predicts that the rate of kinetic energy dissipation in a turbulent flow can remain positive as viscosity tends to zero. In 2023, Bru\`e and De Lellis used quasi-self-similar mixing to construct solutions of the forced three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations exhibiting anomalous dissipation. In this paper, we show that anomalous dissipation can still occur for a flow with spiral geometry in an annulus. In the horizontal plane, we wind a radial segment into a two-turn spiral and then apply alternating shears. After each pair of shears, the image of the segment shares a subarc of positive length with the original spiral. We compare the vertical velocity with sine profiles whose angular period halves with each pair. After the horizontal flow stops, diffusion damps the final profile. By embedding this planar construction into the $(2+\frac{1}{2})$-dimensional framework, we obtain smooth solutions of the three-dimensional equations with the same smooth initial datum. For a sequence of viscosities tending to zero, their dissipation over a fixed subannulus and one vertical period has a uniform positive lower bound, and their forces converge in $C^\alpha$ uniformly in time for every $0<\alpha<1$. We use this spiral construction to produce solutions of the forced three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations that exhibit anomalous dissipation.
item.dc:creator: Changhong Li

item.title: A shock-fitting approach to high-order simulation of viscous hypersonic flows based on inviscid implicit shock tracking
item.description: arXiv:2611.29564v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work presents a framework for computing viscous, shock-dominated flows at high Mach and Reynolds numbers in which the bow shock is located by inviscid implicit shock tracking and then treated as a boundary of the viscous computation. The high-order implicit shock tracking (HOIST) method is applied to the Euler equations on a coarse, shock-agnostic mesh to produce a shock-aligned mesh and the shock geometry; the elements upstream of the shock are discarded, the post-shock domain is remeshed to resolve the boundary layer, and the compressible Navier-Stokes equations are solved on it with a high-order interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method, with the post-shock state prescribed along the shock boundary by the oblique shock relations. Because the shock structure is never resolved, the approach requires neither the extreme element compression nor the specialized formulations that fully coupled viscous shock tracking demands at these conditions; the tracking optimization is confined to the coarse inviscid mesh, and the viscous computation involves no mesh unknowns and no additional nonlinear stabilization. The framework is demonstrated on a Mach 10.6 axisymmetric blunt cone, a Mach 17.6 cylinder, and a Mach 5 sphere in three dimensions, with surface pressure and heat flux in good agreement with experimental measurements and reference computations.
item.dc:creator: Huijing Dong, Alexander M. Perez Reyes, Matthew J. Zahr

item.title: Coarse-Grained Description of Stochastic Neutron Transport in Highly Heterogeneous Reactor Media via Non-Local Feller Boundary Functionals
item.description: arXiv:2611.29680v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents a novel hierarchical coarse-graining framework to model non-Markovian neutron transport within the ultra-heterogeneous, multi-phase subcooled nucleate boiling layer of a nuclear reactor core. By applying Feller's subordination theory to continuous-time random walks, microscopic fluid fluctuations and vapor bubble dynamics are rigorously integrated into macroscopic transport operators through the apparatus of Complete Bernstein Functions (CBF). A modified non-local Fick's law is derived using a $P_1$-Legendre polynomial expansion, mapping the fractal porosity and structural phase boundaries into a stochastically renormalized effective diffusion coefficient. The thermodynamic consistency of the model is grounded within Chentsov's statistical manifolds, demonstrating that granular Poisson-like shot noise yields a geometric-exponential family of distributions characterized by a constant negative information curvature. To evaluate operational safety margins under transient conditions, a generalized Lyapunov functional with a quadratic memory kernel is constructed, and a complex decomposition of the transfer function $H(\omega)$ is performed. The resulting analytical limits are parameterized for a WWER-1000 core layout and translated into an engineering computational sequence suitable for implementation in Mathcad Prime 8 to diagnose the onset of Hopf bifurcations and spatial power oscillations.
item.dc:creator: V. V. Ryazanov

item.title: Topological analysis of permeability tensor in anisotropic porous media
item.description: arXiv:2611.29731v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The permeability of an anisotropic porous medium is a tensor whose off-diagonal components, which describe the deflection of the macroscopic flux away from the driving force, are small and change sign under reflections. We ask whether direction-aware topological data analysis can predict the full permeability tensor of three-dimensional porous media directly from their geometry. We introduce two direction-aware topological descriptors for flow problems: a cone-based filtration, adapted from our earlier work on the elastic stiffness tensor, and a throat-scale filtration built on the distance transform of the pore space. Using permeability tensors computed with the lattice Boltzmann method, we compare them with a comprehensive set of non-topological baselines, comprising statistical microstructure descriptors and physics-based permeability estimators. The topological descriptors are most informative for the off-diagonal components, which the baselines capture least well. There the throat-scale filtration alone outperforms every non-topological descriptor set, including the union of all statistical descriptors and physics-based estimators, and adding it to the baselines consistently improves the prediction. We also confirm the approach on real rock data.
item.dc:creator: Rafa{\l} Topolnicki, Pawe{\l} D{\l}otko, Maciej Matyka

item.title: Cyclic changes of frame for designing non-retracing verification cases for numerical interface tracking
item.description: arXiv:2611.30464v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A forward-backward deformation test supplies an exact final interface, but retracing can allow errors from the two halves to cancel. We construct alternative tests by superposing a cyclic change of frame on the same base deformation. The frame returns to its starting pose, preserving the exact final phase and the deformation history up to rigid placement. A small returning translation can keep trajectories close to the retraced ones. A full rotation about a fixed centre or axis gives closed paths with nonzero winding for material labels that stay off that centre or axis. For incompressible base fields the transformed velocity is divergence-free. We construct discretely solenoidal face fluxes for geometric volume-of-fluid advection by circulating the transformed potential. In three TwoPhaseFlow benchmarks, with a shared time grid for each pair, a full-turn frame increased the final cell-average shape discrepancy in all 30 comparisons, with a median factor of 1.50. The fitted convergence exponent decreased in each of the six benchmark-reconstruction comparisons over the tested grids.
item.dc:creator: Dieter Bothe, Tomislav Mari\'c

item.title: Mass-conservative and phase-consistent transport of phase-confined scalars in front tracking
item.description: arXiv:2611.30693v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In front-tracking multiphase-flow simulations, the Lagrangian front defines the interface geometry and phase regions, while phase-confined scalars are transported independently on a fixed Eulerian mesh. This separation can make the scalar inconsistent with the tracked interface: even a conservative high-order scheme smears the scalar across the interface, leaks it into the other phase and distorts near-interface concentrations despite conserving total mass. We present a transport method that maintains consistency between the scalar and the tracked front while preserving global mass conservation. Instead of the cell-averaged concentration, the method transports the phase-averaged concentration, which is smooth across the interface. This concentration is obtained by dividing the cell-averaged concentration by the phase fraction, extended linearly across the interface and advected. The cell-averaged concentration is rebuilt by multiplying the transported concentration by the front's volume-preserving phase fraction. Because this rebuild can alter the total mass, a uniform shift of the phase-averaged concentration restores it. The method is compared with direct transport of the cell-averaged concentration by the same scheme in five three-dimensional cases: three drops (in translation, in a reversible vortex and with a localized source) and a rising bubble with and without dissolved surfactant. In the four cases without surfactant it reduces the error against the exact solution by more than a factor of ten at the finest resolution and converges faster for the drops. In the surfactant-laden bubble, direct transport leaks 5.5-24% of the surfactant into the wake, depending on resolution, whereas the proposed method keeps it in the bubble.
item.dc:creator: Ayman Mazloum, Gabriele Gennari, Fabian Denner, Berend van Wachem

item.title: A Fitch-Based Wind Farm Parameterization for CM1: Implementation, Validation, and Impacts on Convection Initiation
item.description: arXiv:2611.30806v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We implement a Fitch-based wind farm parameterization in Cloud Model 1 (CM1), representing turbines as elevated momentum sinks and turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) sources within the rotor-swept layer, with optimizations for computational efficiency and parallel execution. Direct comparison with the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model shows close agreement in the magnitude and spatial structure of wind-speed deficits and TKE enhancement. Diurnal simulations also capture the known dependence of boundary layer responses on atmospheric stability, further supporting the consistency of the implementation. Under stable conditions, the wind farm produces coherent spatial patterns in near-surface wind speed and temperature that extend well beyond the farm. In idealized simulations under conditions favorable for convection, large turbines promote convection initiation tens of kilometers downstream, earlier than in the no-farm simulation. Analysis identifies turbulent entrainment of warmer air across the boundary layer top as the dominant source of an elongated downstream warm band, with a smaller contribution from enhanced surface sensible heat flux. Secondary circulations develop across this warm band and provide sustained low-level lifting. A gravity wave generated by the wind farm supplies the initial vertical perturbation, which intensifies as it is advected downstream within an ascending branch of these circulations and develops into a localized deep convective updraft.
item.dc:creator: Jianxiang Li, Zhiyong Meng

item.title: Fifth-order KdV solitary waves in a nonlinear electrical transmission line
item.description: arXiv:2611.31074v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We report the controlled experimental observation of solitary waves governed by the fifth-order dispersion Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation. To achieve vanishing cubic dispersion, we use a mutual inductive coupling between nearest-neighbor inductors within a nonlinear electrical transmission line. We then experimentally characterize the resulting solitary waves through direct spatiotemporal measurements of the dispersion relation, its oscillatory tail profiles, amplitude-width scaling, and amplitude-velocity relation, finding good agreement with semi-analytical predictions. Collision experiments between two (co- or counter-propagating) solitary waves also show that their self-similar profile persists after interaction, up to a time shift. Dissipation effects are also quantified.
item.dc:creator: Loic Fache, Filip Novkoski, Eric Falcon

item.title: Lagrangian Attention Tensor Networks for Velocity Gradient Statistical Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2502.07078v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Direct numerical simulation of turbulence at realistic Reynolds numbers is still beyond current computational capability, necessitating models that reduce the number of resolved spatial scales. Improving these models requires better models of the statistical dynamics of the Velocity Gradient Tensor (VGT) at the Kolmogorov scale. Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) has found considerable success in exploiting large datasets generated from direct numerical simulation (DNS) of Navier-Stokes to improve models for the evolution of the VGT. Using the intimate connection between VGT evolution and fluid deformation, we augment a Tensor Basis Neural Network (TBNN) closure with learned Lagrangian memory kernels, and name the result Lagrangian Attention Tensor Networks (LATN). Trained on single-time (tangent) data, Lagrangian memory is strongly predictive: it lowers the error of the pressure Hessian by 43% and markedly improves its eigenvector alignment, with the most useful history spanning about half a Kolmogorov time. These \textit{a-priori} gains, however, do not translate into improved \textit{a-posteriori} prediction. We therefore inject the memory features into the first layer of a frozen, pre-trained TBNN and train \textit{only the memory} on model rollouts, against a distributional objective. We integrate the model for nine Kolmogorov times from DNS initial conditions and evaluate it with single- and multi-time statistics of the DNS. The resulting LATN retains the trunk's single-time accuracy while improving the long-time statistics: the topology, magnitude and tail distributions of the VGT, and the alignment of vorticity with the strain rate.
item.dc:creator: Criston Hyett, Yifeng Tian, Michael Woodward, Misha Stepanov, Chris Fryer, Daniel Livescu, Michael Chertkov

item.title: Maximal spreading of impacting viscoelastic droplets
item.description: arXiv:2601.15246v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Droplet impact and spreading on solid substrates are well understood for Newtonian fluids, yet how viscoelasticity alone modifies the maximal spreading remains unclear. Here, we isolate the role of viscoelasticity by performing impact experiments with Boger fluids of comparable viscosity and surface tension but different relaxation times. For a wide range of conditions, viscoelastic droplets follow a similar behavior to Newtonian ones{, showcasing the same leading-order inertia--capillary scalings}; however, their maximal spreading diameter is significantly reduced compared with the Newtonian behavior when the Deborah number is of order unity. This reduction is non-monotonic in the relaxation time: droplets with larger relaxation times recover Newtonian-like maximal spreading within experimental uncertainty. We rationalize these observations using an energy-balance model that includes a viscoelastic energy-storage term. The scaling argument obtained from this model explains the reported reduction in maximal spreading and identifies the range of fluid properties for which the strongest viscoelastic effects emerge.
item.dc:creator: Orr Avni, Dongyue Wang, Mithun Ravisankar, Roberto Zenit

item.title: Preconditioned Adjoint Data Assimilation for Two-Dimensional Decaying and Forced Turbulence
item.description: arXiv:2602.14016v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Adjoint-based data assimilation for turbulent Navier-Stokes flows is limited by backward adjoint growth and increasing dominance of small-scale structures, which degrade reconstruction of initial conditions from sparse measurements. We show that the relative weighting of spectral components can be systematically controlled by redefining the inner product under which the adjoint operator is defined. The resulting Fourier-space weighting kernel acts as a preconditioner for the optimization. Specific kernels correspond to fractional integration or diffusion operators on the initial condition. Numerical experiments show that flow-dependent kernel selection substantially improves reconstruction stability and accuracy: exponential kernels suppress high-wavenumber contributions, whereas a fractional integral kernel is particularly effective for forced Kolmogorov flow. Ensemble statistics of adjoint fields reveal scale-dependent backward growth rates, explaining the instability of the standard formulation and how spectral preconditioning attenuates incoherent small-scale amplification.
item.dc:creator: Hongyi Ke, Zejian You, Qi Wang

item.title: Deep Learning of Solver-Aware Turbulence Closures from Nudged LES Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2604.23874v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The differentiable physics paradigm may be leveraged as an a-posteriori approach for discovering turbulence closure models by embedding a neural network parameterization directly inside the solver and optimizing it given potentially sparse target data. This addresses a key limitation of a-priori learning where direct numerical simulation (DNS) data is used to approximate the subgrid stress with the assumption of a low-pass filter. Closures trained in this a-priori manner frequently lead to unstable deployments due to the mismatch between the assumed filter and the effect of numerical discretizations and coarse-graining. In comparison, while typically stable during deployment, a-posteriori learning incurs high computational costs due to the need to backpropagate through a large eddy simulation (LES) solver. Furthermore, a-posteriori methods are challenging to apply broadly since they require significant modification of existing solvers. Finally, both approaches are limited when generalization is desired across different numerical schemes with their implicit filtering characteristics. In this work, we present a deep-learning approach for turbulence closure modeling built on the continuous data assimilation framework. Our approach enables the a-priori training of closures using DNS data observed only at coarse-grid points without modifying or differentiating through the LES solver, while preserving stability during deployment for the recovery of long-term statistics. We focus on the model's ability to adapt to different discretizations by explicitly conditioning it on the numerical scheme. We use two- and three-dimensional canonical cases to test our framework and show that the learned correction systematically tracks the discretization error of the coarse solver.

item.title: Influence of Ideal, Cubic, and Multiparameter Helmholtz Equations of State on the Static and Dynamic Performance of Porous Aerostatic Journal Bearings
item.description: arXiv:2610.27840v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Porous aerostatic gas bearings are commonly modeled using the ideal-gas law, although non-ideal thermodynamic behavior may become relevant for alternative working fluids. This study quantifies the influence of the thermodynamic closure on the stationary and dynamic response of porous aerostatic journal bearings. A finite-volume formulation couples the compressible Reynolds equation with three-dimensional Darcy flow, retaining transient gas storage in both domains. Density is used as the primary thermodynamic variable, allowing the ideal-gas law, three cubic equations of state---van der Waals, Soave--Redlich--Kwong, and Peng--Robinson---and multiparameter Helmholtz equations of state (EOS) to be evaluated within an otherwise unchanged bearing model. Dry air and the refrigerants R1234yf and R1234ze(E) are considered as working fluids to assess the influence of the thermodynamic closure across fluids with different degrees of non-ideal behavior. For air, EOS-induced differences remain negligible over the investigated range. For the refrigerants, the ideal-gas approximation produces several-percent deviations, with supplied mass flow and dynamic force response being particularly sensitive. The cubic equations substantially reduce these deviations, with the employed Peng--Robinson formulation providing the closest agreement with the Helmholtz reference for both refrigerants at a computational cost comparable to the other cubic models. The results identify density and differential compressibility as the main thermodynamic quantities governing the propagation of EOS errors into mass transport and transient gas storage.
item.dc:creator: Laurenz Stellmach, Steffen Nitzschke, Elmar Woschke

item.title: CBTV: Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry for Dense Granular Flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.31883v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In a dense granular flow, a particle that moves more than about half the spacing between frames is easily confused with a neighbour, and so dense flows are recorded at high frame rates. We present Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry (CBTV) for particles of a few distinct colours. CBTV first matches small groups of neighbours by position and colour. It then links the remaining particles by relaxation particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) among particles of the same colour, with a search radius set in each frame from the detections. CBTV was compared with ten published trackers on 15 simulated granular flows, with every tracker given the same detections and one global setting. At 2.8 to 13 diameters per frame, on four flows, CBTV keeps 0.595 of the links, against 0.338 for the best published tracker on each cell. It leads that tracker on every cell outside a rotating drum, where every method fails, and trails on none. CBTV was configured on these four flows with their ground truth in view. At steps 1 to 8, on 45 benchmark cases not used in its tuning, CBTV leads the best published tracker on 14 cases and ties on 31, with no deficit. This test is not fully out of sample, because one setting was fixed after a look at part of the benchmark. The ties lie at small displacements. On two unseen flows, a colour-gated relaxation variant built in this work kept more links than CBTV on average. All tests are simulated.
item.dc:creator: Kaveeshan Thurairajah, Zhao Pan

item.title: Construction of a Deployable Closure Model for the Transport of Turbulence Dissipation Rate with Hard-Constrained Physics-Informed Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.23539v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a hard-constrained physics-informed machine learning (PIML) method for constructing a deployable closure model for the transport of turbulence dissipation rate. The framework is built from modules, each performing a single task. The closure module represents the closure with a small network, while the state module represents the flow state during training. The closure network is coupled to the state network through the governing equation residuals. This coupling allows us to learn the closure without using reference closure values as training targets. The coordinate module learns monotone input coordinates that help both networks resolve sharp changes. Within the network architecture, the boundary condition (BC) module imposes boundary values exactly using the Theory of Functional Connections, and the realizability module keeps the closure realizable. We study decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT) and learn $\psi$, the closure function governing dissipation rate decay, from trajectories obtained in experiments and direct numerical simulations. Here, the state module is a Deep Operator Network (DeepONet), the BC module imposes the initial state and the closure's low and high Reynolds number limits, and the realizability module ensures growth of the Taylor microscale. The framework reduces the root mean square of the closure variation across ten random seeds by about 95\% relative to the unconstrained model over the training and held-out range. The deployed 18-parameter closure network requires only the Taylor scale Reynolds number $Re_{\lambda_g}$ and can be exported as a standalone C function.
