item.title: Global Recovery from Local Data: Interior Nudging for 2D Navier-Stokes equations in a Physical Domain
item.description: arXiv:2601.11831v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In many real-world applications of data assimilation (DA), the strategic placement of observers is crucial for effective and efficient forecasting. Motivated by practical constraints in sensor deployment, we show that global recovery of the flow field can be achieved using observations available only in a subregion of the domain, possibly far from the boundary. We focus on the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations posed in a bounded physical domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions. Building on the continuous data assimilation framework of Azouani, Olson, and Titi (2014), we rigorously prove that the assimilated solution converges globally to the true solution under suitable conditions on the nudging parameter, spatial resolution, and the geometry of the observation region, specifically, when the maximum distance from any point in the domain to the observational subregion is bounded by a constant multiple of \( \nu^{1/2} \) (in terms of scaling). Our computational results, conducted via finite element methods over complex geometries, support the theoretical findings and reveal even greater robustness in practice. Specifically, synchronization with the true solution is achieved even when the observational subregion lies farther from the rest of the domain than the theoretical threshold permits. Across all three tested scenarios, the local nudging algorithm performs comparably to full-domain assimilation, reaching global accuracy up to machine precision. Interestingly, observational data near the boundary are found to be largely uninformative. This demonstrates that full observability is not necessary: carefully chosen interior observations, even far from the boundary, can suffice.
item.dc:creator: Rui Fang, Ali Pakzad

item.title: Structural and Lagrangian properties of analogue ensembles to characterize multifractality of stochastic processes
item.description: arXiv:2605.08155v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a framework for the scale-invariance characterization of stochastic processes in reconstructed finite-dimensional spaces. This framework analyses the structural and dynamical properties of the reconstructed space and is based on a Takens embedding reconstruction followed by the definition of ensembles of analogue states. First, we specify a collection of target states densely sampling the full embedding space. For each target state, we search for the ensemble of its k-nearest neighbors, its k-best analogues, and we analyze its volume and dynamics. On the one hand, we study the probability distribution of the volumes and relate its mean and variance to the scale-invariance properties of the stochastic process. On the second hand, we study the Lagrangian properties of the analogues by characterizing how they disperse in time. More particularly, we study the volume occupied by the analogue's successors in function of time and of their initial volume. The main contribution of this paper is to highlight the link between these dynamical properties and the scale-invariance features of the process. We analyze two types of stationary and dissipative 1-dimensional scale-invariant processes: regularized fractional Brownian motion and regularized multifractal random walk. For both processes, the structure and dynamics of the embedding space are determined by their scale-invariant properties.
item.dc:creator: Carlos Granero-Belinchon (ODYSSEY, IMT Atlantique - MEE, Lab-STICC\_OSE)

item.title: Peristaltic Flow in Compressible, Ideal Magnetohydrodynamics: A Mechanism For Solar Spicules
item.description: arXiv:2606.09626v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present an analytical model for peristaltic transport within compressible, ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD). By employing a small-amplitude perturbation expansion, under a thin-tube long-wavelength approximation with a uniform axial background magnetic field, we study non-linear coupling between thermodynamic pressure variations and Maxwell's magnetic tension stresses. The resulting net time-averaged conserved mass flux $\langle \dot{M} \rangle$ is calculated. When applied to solar chromospheric spicules under equipartition constraints ($\beta \sim 1$), where sound speed matches the Alfv{\'e}n speed, we find $\langle \dot{M} \rangle = 8\epsilon^2/(M^2-1)^2$. Because the denominator remains strictly positive across all operational supersonic Mach numbers ($M \approx 2\text{--}10$), upward-propagating mechanical disturbances drive a highly directional, collimated upward flow which we interpret as a spicule. Estimates show that for observationally realistic magnetosonic waves with amplitudes of $\approx 10\%$, the peristaltic mechanism generates a localized mass flux up to $\approx 100$ times that of the solar wind. We show that because high-Mach waves suffer strong compressible choking, small-amplitude perturbations preferentially select low-supersonic modes ($M \approx 1.05\text{--}2.0$) to drive spicule-level mass loading. We propose an explicit observational signature of this mechanism, wherein the launch of individual spicular jets is directly preceded by magnetosonic wave trains detectable as localized intensity modulations. Beyond solar chromospheric application, the model may be applicable to traveling magnetic field pinches in laboratory plasma devices and astrophysical mass-loading processes in stellar winds and inner regions of magnetized accretion disks.
item.dc:creator: D. Tsiklauri

item.title: Resonant lunar tides of Earth's core and basal magma ocean
item.description: arXiv:2606.16340v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Earth's magnetic field is generated by fluid motion in the liquid-metal core and has been active for billions of years. However, prior to the onset of inner-core growth, the sources of mechanical power that drove the geodynamo remain uncertain. During this period, the core may have been overlain by a basal magma ocean (BMO), creating two immiscible fluid layers separated by a density interface, beneath the solid mantle. We develop a theory for lunar tides in this core--BMO system, in which the tidal potential acts on the density contrast between the two layers. The resulting dynamics differ fundamentally from previous models driven by imposed deformation of the core's bounding envelope. In the inviscid limit, the response transitions from an equilibrium tide to an interfacial gravity wave as forcing frequency increases. The two regimes are separated by a resonance that occurs when the forcing frequency matches the natural frequency of the degree-2, order-2 interfacial mode. The inviscid core flow is formally identical to the canonical elliptical vortex, linking the problem to the theory of elliptical instability. Finite viscosity regularises the resonance, introduces phase lag and generates oscillatory boundary layers. Combined with parameterised models of lunar recession and BMO crystallisation, the theory predicts enhanced core-boundary ellipticity, core-flow speed, magnetic Reynolds number and instability metrics, particularly near resonance. These results identify a previously unexplored mechanism for tidally driven flow in differentiated planetary bodies and show that a BMO can enhance tidal coupling to the core, potentially contributing to dynamo action.
item.dc:creator: Murray B. C. Kiernan, Hamish C. F. C. Hay, David W. Rees Jones, James F. J. Bryson, Richard F. Katz

item.title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs
item.description: arXiv:2611.17141v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Symmetry is a foundational principle of physics: the behavior of a PDE-governed system does not depend on the coordinate frame, unit system, or mesh used to write it down, and neither should a surrogate model. Yet today's leading neural surrogates lack these invariances and fail under simple transformations of the same problem: for models trained on PDEs of cars in one pose (i.e., translation and rotation), rotating the full PDE raises the surface-pressure error from 4% to more than 100%, and re-sampling its boundary raises it to about 30%. We introduce ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention), a slice-attention transformer for steady, boundary-driven PDEs. Because the boundary determines the interior solution, ISLA encodes the posed boundary once into learned slices and evaluates arbitrary interior points independently through a tree-accelerated learned boundary kernel. Inputs are nondimensionalized in scales computed from the boundary, sums over boundary cells are area-weighted quadratures that converge under mesh refinement, and geometry enters only as distances and relative angles to equivariant slice anchors, making the model equivariant to rigid motions and reflections up to optional token subsampling and tree clustering. On AeroZoo, 2,816 3D flows spanning diverse geometries, poses, physical scales, and boundary conditions, ISLA's mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are 1.9 and 2.2 times lower than the best baseline's. On full AirfRANS, ISLA is second only to an explicit boundary-integral network (GLOBE), with errors 1.6 to 2.6 times lower than the better of Transolver's and GeoTransolver's in every field.
item.dc:creator: Peter Sharpe

item.title: AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.17152v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are trained and ranked on single-family, fixed-domain datasets that cannot test the minimum bar for an aerodynamic foundation model: predicting CFD-quality incompressible flow in seconds for new shapes in new enclosures. On DrivAerML, larger models and longer training barely lower Transolver's error; doubling training cases cuts it by about 12% up to 400 cases, exhausting the dataset. We introduce AeroZoo, a benchmark and training corpus of 3,815 time-mean unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (URANS) solutions with a transition model across seven geometry families, eight enclosures, and Reynolds numbers from $10^3$ to $10^8$. Each sample poses a well-posed PDE problem as a solver receives it: boundary meshes grouped by condition type, prescribed values, and fluid properties. The 2,816 time-mean-stable samples form the canonical benchmark: two tasks, mean engineering metrics with an overall flow score $S_{\mathrm{flow}}$ (1.000 for uniform inlet flow), and 22 frozen geometry-disjoint splits holding out shapes, enclosures, boundary-condition layouts, and Reynolds ranges. On the random split, boundary-condition tokens cut GeoTransolver's mean velocity error from 89.8% to 15.2% of inlet speed (uniform flow: 44.0%; $S_{\mathrm{flow}} = 0.290$). ISLA, a boundary-driven transformer, reaches 8.2% ($S_{\mathrm{flow}} = 0.153$; 0.123 with boundary targets), about 6 times mesh-refinement sensitivity. On shared test samples, holding out a geometry family barely changes ISLA's mean velocity error, whereas holding out enclosures or boundary-condition layouts raises it 3.8 to 8.4 times. The dataset is public; the scoring code will be released.
item.dc:creator: Peter Sharpe, Carmelo Gonzales, Corey Adams, Mohammadmehdi Ataei, Sanjay Choudhry
